dialect.name: crag
dialect.title: 'crag' Dialect
dialect.description:
This dialect of MLIR is used to lower descriptions of audio graphs to
LLVM IR for offline evaluation or ahead-of-time compilation.

entries.name: crag.foo
entries.summary: Illustrates how to define an operation.
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.foo` $input attr-dict `:` type($input)
```

The `crag.foo` operation illustrates how to define a new
operation in a dialect. It uses an operation trait to declare that it
has no side effects.

This operation takes an integer argument and returns an integer.

Example:

```mlir
%0 = arith.constant 2 : i32
// Apply the foo operation to %0
%1 = crag.foo %0 : i32
```

Traits: `AlwaysSpeculatableImplTrait`, `SameOperandsAndResultType`

Interfaces: `ConditionallySpeculatable`, `InferTypeOpInterface`, `NoMemoryEffect (MemoryEffectOpInterface)`

Effects: `MemoryEffects::Effect{}`

#### Operands:

| Operand | Description |
| :-----: | ----------- |
| `input` | 32-bit signless integer |

#### Results:

| Result | Description |
| :----: | ----------- |
| `res` | 32-bit signless integer |

entries.name: crag.graph
entries.summary: Audio graph container
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.graph` (`name` `=` $graph_name^ )? `sample_rate` `=` $sample_rate `channels` `=` $channels (`preferred_resampler` `=` $preferred_resampler^)? (`preferred_channel_mixer` `=` $preferred_channel_mixer^)? (`default_visualizer` `=` $default_visualizer^)? $body attr-dict ``` Container operation that holds one region with CRAG processor nodes. The `sample_rate` and `channels` attributes declare the audio format that all audio signals in the graph must conform to. Use `crag.sample_rate` inside the body to obtain the sample rate as an f32 SSA value. A graph may be given a name via `sym_name`, making it a reusable subgraph. Named graphs may declare audio inputs as block arguments on the entry block, e.g.: ```mlir crag.graph name = "my_filter" sample_rate = 48000 channels = 1 { ^bb0(%in: !crag.audio): crag.output %in : !crag.audio } ``` The number of block arguments gives the number of audio inputs; their types define the expected `!crag.audio<...>` mapping. Use `crag.subgraph_ref` to invoke a named graph from within another graph. The optional `preferred_channel_mixer` attribute selects the strategy `crag-inject-channel-mixers` uses to adapt this graph to a host channel count that differs from its native one. It names either a standard-graph mixer (e.g. `"mono_to_stereo"`, `"stereo_to_mono_average"`) for the output-side conversion, or the structural strategy `"parallel"`, which replicates a mono graph's body once per host channel (channel `c` is fed the `c`-th channel of every audio input and the per-channel outputs are joined back into the host layout). `"parallel"` is only valid when the graph's native channel count is 1. The optional `default_visualizer` attribute names the built-in visualizer type to inject when the `crag-inject-visualizer` pass is run without an explicit `--viz-type` option. Valid values are `"oscilloscope"`, `"spectrometer"`, `"phase-correlation"`, `"loudness-meter"`, `"loudness-history"`, and `"compressor-viz"`. #### Attributes:
AttributeMLIR TypeDescription
graph_name::mlir::StringAttrstring attribute
sample_rate::mlir::IntegerAttr32-bit signless integer attribute
channels::mlir::IntegerAttr32-bit signless integer attribute
preferred_resampler::mlir::StringAttrstring attribute
preferred_channel_mixer::mlir::StringAttrstring attribute
default_visualizer::mlir::StringAttrstring attribute

entries.name: crag.include
entries.summary: Import a named crag.graph from an external .mlir file
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.include` $path `as` $graph_name (`params` `=` $params_ns^)? attr-dict ``` Declares that a crag.graph should be imported from an external MLIR file. The `crag-resolve-includes` pass processes this op before any other passes: it loads the referenced file, finds the anonymous (or named) crag.graph inside, clones it into the current module under the name `graph_name`, and removes this op. Once resolved, the imported graph can be called with `crag.subgraph_ref "graph_name"(...)` just like any named local subgraph. The optional `params_ns` attribute, when provided, causes all `crag.param` names in the imported graph to be prefixed with `params_ns + "."` so that they appear as namespaced parameters in the public API (e.g. `"reverb.room_size"` instead of `"room_size"`). This avoids name collisions when the same library graph is included multiple times or alongside graphs that share parameter names. Example: ```mlir // Import reverb graph, exposing its params under the "rev" namespace. crag.include "standard-graphs/freeverb.crag.mlir" as "reverb" params = "rev" // Import without param namespacing: crag.include "standard-graphs/schroeder-reverb.crag.mlir" as "schroeder" crag.graph sample_rate = 48000 channels = 1 { ... %wet = crag.subgraph_ref "reverb"(%dry) : (!crag.audio) -> !crag.audio ... } ``` #### Attributes:
AttributeMLIR TypeDescription
path::mlir::StringAttrstring attribute
graph_name::mlir::StringAttrstring attribute
params_ns::mlir::StringAttrstring attribute

entries.name: crag.subgraph_ref
entries.summary: Reference to a named crag.graph subgraph
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.subgraph_ref` $callee `(` $inputs `)` attr-dict `:` functional-type(operands, results) ``` Invokes a named `crag.graph` with the given audio inputs, producing a single audio output. The callee is identified by the string name given in the target graph's `sym_name` attribute. The referenced graph must exist in the same module, must share the same `sample_rate` and `channels` as the enclosing graph, and the operand types must match the entry-block arguments of the callee. This op is eliminated by the `crag-inline-subgraphs` pass before code generation. Example: ```mlir %out = crag.subgraph_ref "my_filter"(%noise) : (!crag.audio) -> !crag.audio ``` Traits: `AlwaysSpeculatableImplTrait` Interfaces: `ConditionallySpeculatable`, `NoMemoryEffect (MemoryEffectOpInterface)` Effects: `MemoryEffects::Effect{}` #### Attributes:
AttributeMLIR TypeDescription
callee::mlir::StringAttrstring attribute
#### Operands: | Operand | Description | | :-----: | ----------- | | `inputs` | variadic of crag audio signal type | #### Results: | Result | Description | | :----: | ----------- | | `out` | crag audio signal type |

entries.name: crag.texture_output
entries.summary: Declares an image/texture output
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.texture_output` ($viz_name^)? ($texture^ `:` type($texture))? attr-dict ``` Publishes a texture output. The op has two context-dependent forms, distinguished by the parent op (enforced by the verifier): 1. Inside a `crag.visualizer` body (operand REQUIRED): `crag.texture_output %tex : !crag.texture` broadcasts the visualizer's final rendered texture — the canvas the host pulls through `crag_engine_pull_visualizer`. Exactly one per visualizer. 2. Inside a `crag.graph` body (operand FORBIDDEN): a no-operand marker declaring that the graph publishes an image output (its visualizer canvas). Emitted by the engine's session build (`crag_engine_build_mlir`) for graph instances routed into a generic image/window sink; dropped by the audio lowering. The optional `viz_name` selects a specific named `crag.visualizer`; when omitted, the graph's default visualizer is the output. #### Attributes:
AttributeMLIR TypeDescription
viz_name::mlir::StringAttrstring attribute
#### Operands: | Operand | Description | | :-----: | ----------- | | `texture` | crag texture type |

entries.name: crag.block_size
entries.summary: Returns the compile-time audio block size as i64
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.block_size` attr-dict `:` type($value)
```

Returns the number of audio samples per block as a 64-bit integer.
This value is fixed at compile time (typically 512) and is determined
by the `block-size` option passed to `crag-lower-audio-to-tensor`.

`crag.block_size` is useful inside `crag.func` bodies (e.g. the
`metronome` sequencing function) where the block size must be known
to determine whether an event falls within the current block.

Example:
```mlir
%bs = crag.block_size : i64
```

Interfaces: `ConditionallySpeculatable`, `InferTypeOpInterface`, `NoMemoryEffect (MemoryEffectOpInterface)`

Effects: `MemoryEffects::Effect{}`

| :----: | ----------- |
| `value` | 64-bit signless integer |

entries.name: crag.sample_rate
entries.summary: Returns the sample rate of the enclosing crag.graph as f32
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.sample_rate` attr-dict `:` type($value)
```

Returns the sample rate declared on the nearest enclosing `crag.graph`
op as a 32-bit float value.  This is the canonical way to obtain the
sample rate inside a graph body so that the graph remains
self-describing rather than relying on magic constants.

Example:
```mlir
crag.graph sample_rate = 48000 channels = 1 {
  %sr      = crag.sample_rate : f32
  %two     = arith.constant 2.0 : f32
  %half_sr = arith.divf %sr, %two : f32
  ...
}
```

Traits: `AlwaysSpeculatableImplTrait`

Interfaces: `ConditionallySpeculatable`, `InferTypeOpInterface`, `NoMemoryEffect (MemoryEffectOpInterface)`

entries.name: crag.impulse
entries.summary: Generates a unit impulse (Dirac delta) audio signal
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.impulse` (`position` `=` $position^)? attr-dict `:` type($out) ``` Produces a block of audio samples where every sample is 0.0 except for the single sample at the given absolute sample position, which is 1.0. The default `position` is 0, which fires on the very first sample when a `crag.graph` is evaluated. For multi-channel audio the impulse fires on all channels at the specified frame position. This is the audio equivalent of a Dirac delta / Kronecker delta and is primarily used for impulse-response measurement: routing it through any linear time-invariant (LTI) graph yields the graph's impulse response, which fully characterises its frequency-domain behaviour. Example: ```mlir // Impulse at the very first sample (default): %imp = crag.impulse : !crag.audio // Impulse at absolute sample index 100: %imp = crag.impulse position = 100 : !crag.audio ``` Traits: `AlwaysSpeculatableImplTrait` Interfaces: `ConditionallySpeculatable`, `NoMemoryEffect (MemoryEffectOpInterface)` Effects: `MemoryEffects::Effect{}` #### Attributes:
AttributeMLIR TypeDescription
position::mlir::IntegerAttr64-bit signless integer attribute
#### Results: | Result | Description | | :----: | ----------- | | `out` | crag audio signal type |

entries.name: crag.lazy_wavetable
entries.summary: Lazily-rendered wavetable cache for finite subgraphs with infrequent inputs (inserted by crag-fold-infrequent-finite-subgraphs)
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.lazy_wavetable` $table_sym `,` `thunk` `=` $render_thunk `,` `inputs` `=` `(` $inputs `)` `,` `triggers` `=` `(` $triggers `)` `,` `length` `=` $length (`period` `=` $period^)? attr-dict `:` functional-type(operands, results) ``` Reads one audio block from a per-instance wavetable cache that holds the most recently rendered tail (`length` samples per channel) of an extracted finite subgraph. Unlike `crag.wavetable_osc` (which is cyclic and read-only), the cache is rebuilt on demand by calling the symbolically-referenced render thunk whenever any of the subgraph's `infrequent` inputs (params or events) has changed since the last render. Operands: - `inputs` — current values of the captured `infrequent` params and event payloads, in declaration order. These are the scalar arguments forwarded to the render thunk. - `triggers` — `i1` "fired since last render" flags for each captured event input, in declaration order. Used by lowering to compute the dirty bit. Attributes: - `table_sym` — `FlatSymbolRefAttr` referencing the `memref.global` of size `length × channels` that holds the cache. - `render_thunk` — `FlatSymbolRefAttr` referencing the private `func.func` that re-renders the cache from the current `inputs`. - `length` — `I64Attr`, total number of samples in the finite tail per channel. Output past sample `length` is zero. - `period` — `OptionalAttr`. When set, the cached tail is exactly periodic with this divisor of `length`, and lowering may treat this as a `crag.wavetable_osc` (no dirty guard, modular indexing). When unset, lowering emits the dirty guard + non-cyclic playhead read with zeroing past `length`. Runtime semantics (emitted by `CragLowerAudioToTensor`): 1. At the start of each block, compute `rerender = dirty || any(trigger fired) || any(input != its value at the last render)`. Input change detection is by value against per-instance `_lastin_` sibling globals. If `rerender`, call `@render_thunk(inputs..., %table)`, clear the dirty flag, and store the rendered-with input values. 2. The playhead resets to 0 only for dirty/trigger invalidation (a trigger is a fresh musical onset). A changed input alone re-renders the table IN PLACE and playback continues from the current position — mirroring the unfolded graph, where a param change never restarts the envelope, and a knob turned after the tail has finished keeps silence. 3. Read `length`-bounded samples from `%table` at the current playhead, advancing the playhead by the block size and returning zero for sample positions ≥ `length`. This op is produced by the `crag-fold-infrequent-finite-subgraphs` pass and is the natural sibling of `crag.wavetable_osc`: periodic folding handles infinite-but-repeating constant-input chains; this op handles finite-and-non-repeating chains whose only non-constant inputs are annotated `infrequent`. Example: ```mlir %s = crag.lazy_wavetable @crag_lazycache_0_table, thunk = @_crag_lazy_render_0, inputs = (%wet), triggers = (%trig) length = 96000 : (f32, i1) -> !crag.audio ``` Traits: `AttrSizedOperandSegments` #### Attributes:
AttributeMLIR TypeDescription
table_sym::mlir::FlatSymbolRefAttrflat symbol reference attribute
render_thunk::mlir::FlatSymbolRefAttrflat symbol reference attribute
length::mlir::IntegerAttr64-bit signless integer attribute
period::mlir::IntegerAttr64-bit signless integer attribute
#### Operands: | Operand | Description | | :-----: | ----------- | | `inputs` | variadic of any type | | `triggers` | variadic of 1-bit signless integer | #### Results: | Result | Description | | :----: | ----------- | | `out` | crag audio signal type |

entries.name: crag.saw
entries.summary: Sawtooth-wave oscillator
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.saw` $freq `,` $phase attr-dict `:` type($freq) `,` type($phase) `->` type($out)
```

Produces a block of audio samples representing a sawtooth wave that
ramps linearly from -1 to +1 over each period:

    t_norm[n] = frac(freq * n / sample_rate + phase / (2π))
    sample[n] = 2 * t_norm[n] - 1

`freq` is the frequency in Hz and `phase` is the phase offset in
radians.

Example:
```mlir
%saw = crag.saw %freq, %phase : f32, f32 -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
```

Traits: `AlwaysSpeculatableImplTrait`

Interfaces: `ConditionallySpeculatable`, `NoMemoryEffect (MemoryEffectOpInterface)`

Effects: `MemoryEffects::Effect{}`

#### Operands:

| Operand | Description |
| :-----: | ----------- |
| `freq` | 32-bit float |
| `phase` | 32-bit float |

#### Results:

| Result | Description |
| :----: | ----------- |
| `out` | crag audio signal type |

entries.name: crag.sine
entries.summary: Sinusoidal oscillator
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.sine` $freq `,` $phase attr-dict `:` type($freq) `,` type($phase) `->` type($out)
```

Produces a block of audio samples representing a sinusoidal signal:

    sample[n] = sin(2π * freq * n / sample_rate + phase)

`freq` is the frequency in Hz and `phase` is the initial phase offset
in radians.  The output audio type determines the sample rate and
channel count.

Example:
```mlir
crag.graph sample_rate = 48000 channels = 1 {
  %freq  = arith.constant 440.0 : f32
  %phase = arith.constant 0.0   : f32
  %tone  = crag.sine %freq, %phase : f32, f32 -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
  crag.output %tone : !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
}
```

Traits: `AlwaysSpeculatableImplTrait`

Interfaces: `ConditionallySpeculatable`, `NoMemoryEffect (MemoryEffectOpInterface)`

Effects: `MemoryEffects::Effect{}`

entries.name: crag.square
entries.summary: Square-wave oscillator
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.square` $freq `,` $phase `,` $duty attr-dict `:` type($freq) `,` type($phase) `,` type($duty) `->` type($out)
```

Produces a block of audio samples representing a square wave with an
adjustable duty cycle:

    t_norm[n] = frac(freq * n / sample_rate + phase / (2π))
    sample[n] = (t_norm[n] < duty) ? +1.0 : -1.0

`freq` is the frequency in Hz, `phase` is the phase offset in radians,
and `duty` is the duty cycle in [0, 1] (0.5 gives a symmetric square
wave).

Example:
```mlir
%sq = crag.square %freq, %phase, %duty
          : f32, f32, f32 -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
```

entries.name: crag.tri
entries.summary: Triangle-wave oscillator
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.tri` $freq `,` $phase `,` $duty attr-dict `:` type($freq) `,` type($phase) `,` type($duty) `->` type($out)
```

Produces a block of audio samples representing a triangle wave with an
adjustable duty cycle (symmetry point):

    t_norm[n] = frac(freq * n / sample_rate + phase / (2π))
    if t_norm[n] < duty:
      sample[n] = 2 * t_norm[n] / duty - 1
    else:
      sample[n] = 1 - 2 * (t_norm[n] - duty) / (1 - duty)

`freq` is the frequency in Hz, `phase` is the phase offset in radians,
and `duty` in [0, 1] controls the symmetry of the rising/falling slopes
(0.5 gives an isosceles triangle).

Example:
```mlir
%tri = crag.tri %freq, %phase, %duty
           : f32, f32, f32 -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
```

entries.summary: Element-wise multiply two audio signals
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.audio_mul` $lhs `,` $rhs attr-dict `:` type($lhs) `,` type($rhs) `->` type($out)
```

Multiplies the two `!crag.audio` input blocks sample-by-sample and
returns the result as a new audio block.  Both inputs and the result
must have the same `!crag.audio` type.

This is the primary building block for polynomial waveshapers: applying
`crag.audio_mul` twice with the same operand produces x², and chaining
with a second multiply gives x³, enabling cubic and higher-order
distortion curves.

Example:
```mlir
// Square every sample: y[n] = x[n] * x[n]
%x2 = crag.audio_mul %x, %x
          : !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>, !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>
            -> !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>

// Cube every sample: y[n] = x[n]^3
%x3 = crag.audio_mul %x2, %x
          : !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>, !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>
            -> !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>
```

entries.name: crag.channel_join
entries.summary: Combine multiple audio signals into one multi-channel audio signal
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.channel_join` $inputs attr-dict `:` functional-type(operands, results)
```

Interleaves the samples of two or more `!crag.audio` inputs into a
single multi-channel `!crag.audio` output.  All inputs must share the
same sample rate and element type.  The number of channels in the
result equals the sum of the channel counts of all inputs.

Channels are appended in operand order.  For example, joining a
1-channel left signal and a 1-channel right signal gives a 2-channel
stereo output where channel 0 = left and channel 1 = right.

Layout: for output frame `f` and an input `k` with `ck` channels
starting at output channel `base_k`:
  out[f * outChannels + base_k + c] = in_k[f * ck + c]

This op is the dual of `crag.channel_slice`.

Example:
```mlir
// Combine a left and right mono signal into stereo.
%stereo = crag.channel_join %left, %right
              : (!crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>, !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>)
                -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 2>
```

entries.name: crag.scale
entries.summary: Multiply each sample of an audio signal by a scalar gain
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.scale` $input `,` $gain attr-dict `:` type($input) `,` type($gain) `->` type($out)
```

`gain` value and returns the result as a new audio block with the same
type.  A `gain` of 1.0 is the identity; values less than 1.0 attenuate
and values greater than 1.0 amplify.  Negative values invert the phase.

`gain` < 1.0 ensures stability) and wet/dry mixing.

```mlir
%g    = arith.constant 0.75 : f32

                    -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
```

entries.name: crag.get_filter_coeffs
entries.summary: Compute IIR filter coefficients from design parameters
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.get_filter_coeffs` $cutoff `order` `=` $order (`q` `=` $q^)? (`q_runtime` `=` $q_runtime^ `:` type($q_runtime))? `type` `=` $filter_type attr-dict `:` type($cutoff) `,` type($feedback) `,` type($feedforward) ``` Computes IIR feedback and feedforward filter coefficients from a normalized frequency cutoff, a desired filter order, and a filter type. The cutoff must be strictly between 0 and 1 (where 1 = Nyquist). When the cutoff operand is a compile-time constant, this is verified statically; otherwise it is a runtime responsibility. Supported filter types: `"lowpass"`, `"highpass"`, `"bandpass"`, `"notch"`, and `"two_pole_resonator"`. For `"two_pole_resonator"` the op additionally requires the quality factor, supplied as **either** the compile-time scalar attribute `q` (baked into the coefficient computation) **or** the runtime `q_runtime` f32 operand (recomputed every block); exactly one of the two must be present, and `order` must be `2`. Use the attribute form when the resonator's bandwidth is fixed at codegen time and the runtime form when it depends on a host-controlled parameter (e.g. a modal-synthesis `dampen` knob that increases per-mode damping while a finger is muting the object). Both forms share the same math: the resulting filter is a constant-Q biquad resonator with poles at radius `r = exp(-π·cutoff / (2·Q))` and angle `θ = π·cutoff`: y[n] = x[n] + 2·r·cos(θ)·y[n−1] − r²·y[n−2] For modal-synthesis use, the natural mapping from a continuous-time second-order mode with frequency `f_hz` and damping ratio `ζ` is: cutoff = f_hz / (sample_rate / 2) Q = 1 / (2·ζ) Example (lowpass): ```mlir crag.graph sample_rate = 48000 channels = 1 { %cutoff_hz = crag.param "cutoff_hz" min = 20.0 max = 20000.0 default = 1200.0 : f32 %sr = crag.sample_rate : f32 %two = arith.constant 2.0 : f32 %nyquist = arith.divf %sr, %two : f32 %norm = arith.divf %cutoff_hz, %nyquist : f32 %fb, %ff = crag.get_filter_coeffs %norm order = 2 type = "lowpass" : f32, !crag.coeff_vec, !crag.coeff_vec ... } ``` Example (modal two-pole resonator, baked Q): ```mlir %norm = arith.constant 0.05 : f32 // f_hz / (sr/2) %fb, %ff = crag.get_filter_coeffs %norm order = 2 q = 50.0 type = "two_pole_resonator" : f32, !crag.coeff_vec, !crag.coeff_vec ``` Example (modal two-pole resonator, runtime Q driven by a `dampen` param): ```mlir %dampen = crag.param "dampen" min = 0.0 max = 1.0 default = 0.0 : f32 %zeta0 = arith.constant 0.01 : f32 // ζ baseline for this mode %dzmax = arith.constant 0.10 : f32 // Δζ when dampen = 1 %dz = arith.mulf %dzmax, %dampen : f32 %zeff = arith.addf %zeta0, %dz : f32 %two = arith.constant 2.0 : f32 %twozef = arith.mulf %two, %zeff : f32 %one = arith.constant 1.0 : f32 %qeff = arith.divf %one, %twozef : f32 // Q = 1/(2ζ) %norm = arith.constant 0.05 : f32 %fb, %ff = crag.get_filter_coeffs %norm order = 2 q_runtime = %qeff : f32 type = "two_pole_resonator" : f32, !crag.coeff_vec, !crag.coeff_vec ``` Traits: `AlwaysSpeculatableImplTrait` Interfaces: `ConditionallySpeculatable`, `NoMemoryEffect (MemoryEffectOpInterface)` Effects: `MemoryEffects::Effect{}` #### Attributes:
AttributeMLIR TypeDescription

filter_type::mlir::StringAttrstring attribute
q::mlir::FloatAttr32-bit float attribute
#### Operands: | Operand | Description | | :-----: | ----------- | | `cutoff` | 32-bit float | | `q_runtime` | 32-bit float | #### Results: | Result | Description | | :----: | ----------- | | `feedback` | crag filter coefficient vector type | | `feedforward` | crag filter coefficient vector type |

entries.summary: SR latch with persistent boolean state across process() calls
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.latch` $set `,` $reset attr-dict `:` type($set) `,` type($reset) `->` type($state)
```

Implements a dominant-set SR (set-reset) latch whose state is maintained
across `crag_process()` calls.  Each unique instance keeps its own
persistent `i32` global (initialized to 1 — set, so playback begins
immediately without an explicit start event).

Behaviour per block:
  - If `set` is `true`:   state ← 1  (set dominates reset)
  - Else if `reset` is `true`: state ← 0
  - Otherwise: state unchanged

Returns the (possibly updated) latch state as `i1`.

Example:
```mlir
%start_fired, %start_at = crag.event_void "start" : i1, i32
%stop_fired,  %stop_at  = crag.event_void "stop"  : i1, i32
%playing = crag.latch %start_fired, %stop_fired : i1, i1 -> i1
```

entries.name: crag.smooth
entries.summary: Per-block first-order IIR scalar envelope smoother with asymmetric attack/release
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.smooth` $value `,` $attack_ms `,` $release_ms attr-dict `:`
              type($value) `,` type($attack_ms) `,` type($release_ms) `->` type($smoothed)
```

Applies an asymmetric first-order IIR (leaky-integrator) filter to a
scalar `f32` value at block rate, maintaining persistent state across
`crag_process()` calls.  Each unique instance of this op maintains its
own state variable (a single `f32` global, initialized to 0.0).

The smoothing behaviour depends on the direction of change:
  - If the new value is **greater** than the stored state (envelope is
    growing), the `attack_ms` time constant governs the update speed.
  - If the new value is **less than or equal** to the stored state
    (envelope is decaying), the `release_ms` time constant governs.

Time constants are specified in milliseconds.  The effective one-pole
coefficient is computed from the time constant, the block size, and the
graph's sample rate at compile time:

    coef = exp( −block_size / (time_ms × sample_rate / 1000) )

A `time_ms` of 0 gives an instant response (coef → 0), while very
large values approach a hold (coef → 1).

Typical use: smoothing the output of `crag.rms` or `crag.peak` to form
a compressor / limiter envelope detector.

Example:
```mlir
%env = crag.smooth %level, %attack_ms, %release_ms
           : f32, f32, f32 -> f32
```

entries.name: crag.audio_input
entries.summary: Declares a named audio input slot for the primary graph
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.audio_input` $name (`default` `=` $default_signal^)? (`preferred_channel_mixer` `=` $preferred_channel_mixer^)? attr-dict `:` type($out) ``` Declares a named audio input port on the unnamed (top-level) `crag.graph`. The host binds an upstream audio buffer to this slot by name (or by index, in slot-first-appearance order), and on each render block the compiled binary reads the bound buffer and presents it as the `!crag.audio` SSA value produced by this op. This op is the canonical way to author primary-graph audio inputs. Existing graphs that declare inputs as block-arguments on the unnamed top-level graph are equivalent: the `crag-canonicalize-primary-inputs` pass rewrites them into `crag.audio_input` ops with auto-generated names (`input0`, `input1`, …), so all downstream passes see a single canonical form. Named library graphs (those with a `name = "..."` attribute) must continue to use block-arguments for their inputs; `crag.audio_input` is only valid in the unnamed top-level graph. Properties: - `name` is unique within the enclosing graph. - The result `!crag.audio` type's sample rate must either be `0` (inherit from the enclosing graph) or match the enclosing graph's `sample_rate` attribute. - The result `!crag.audio` type's channel count is the channel count delivered by the host on the bound buffer. When it differs from the enclosing graph's `channels` attribute, the `crag-inject-channel-mixers` pass injects a channel-mixing graph immediately after this op (so downstream ops always consume the graph's internal channel count). A value of `0` is a placeholder that `crag-resolve-channel-counts` resolves to the graph's `channels` attribute (no mixer needed in that case). - The optional `default_signal` attribute selects the deterministic waveform produced when the host has not bound any upstream buffer to this slot. Only `"silence"` (zero-fill) is currently defined. - The optional `preferred_channel_mixer` attribute selects the standard-graph mixer used by `crag-inject-channel-mixers` when this input's channel count differs from the enclosing graph's channels. Mirrors the same-named attribute on `crag.graph` (which controls the output-side mixer). Example: ```mlir crag.graph sample_rate = 48000 channels = 1 { // Host delivers stereo; pass injects stereo_to_mono_average. %in = crag.audio_input "in" preferred_channel_mixer = "stereo_to_mono_average" : !crag.audio crag.output %in : !crag.audio } ``` Traits: `AlwaysSpeculatableImplTrait` Interfaces: `ConditionallySpeculatable`, `NoMemoryEffect (MemoryEffectOpInterface)` Effects: `MemoryEffects::Effect{}` #### Attributes:

entries.summary: Read a single sample from a captured audio block (visualizer)
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.audio_read` $audio `,` $index attr-dict `:` type($audio) `,` type($index) `->` type($value)
```

Reads the `f32` sample at `index` from a `!crag.audio` block.  Inside a
`crag.visualizer` body the audio operand is the visualizer's captured
input block (its `crag.audio_input`), so `crag.audio_read` is the
element-wise primitive an imperative visualizer uses to plot that block
— the building block for an oscilloscope trace, a peak meter, a phase
scatter, or a spectrum (reading the per-bin FFT magnitudes a co-located
`crag.fft` deposits into the capture buffer).

The index is a raw element index into the capture buffer.  Out-of-range
indices read `0.0`.  The buffer length is the visualizer capture size
(`crag.block_size` for a mono PCM capture; `block_size * 2` for an
interleaved stereo capture; `block_size/2 + 1` for an FFT-magnitude
capture).

Example (oscilloscope column):
```mlir
%audio = crag.audio_input "audio" : !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>
%n     = crag.block_size : i64
// sampleIdx = (x * n) / W
%v     = crag.audio_read %audio, %sampleIdx
```

Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.sample_oneshot` $sampler `,` $start `,` $end `,` $fired `,` $sample_offset attr-dict `:` type($sampler) `,` type($start) `,` type($end) `,` type($fired) `,` type($sample_offset) `->` type($out)
```

Plays the sampler slice `[start, end)` exactly once, beginning at the
most recent firing of the supplied event, and outputs silence before
the first trigger and after the slice has been exhausted.  Firing the
event again restarts playback from `start` (a fresh one-shot voice).

Per-sample semantics (with `n` the absolute stream frame and
`trigFrame` the stream frame of the most recent fire, latched in
per-op state across blocks):

    pos    = n - trigFrame
    out[n] = (fired at least once && 0 <= pos < end - start)
               ? data[start + pos] : 0.0

This is the op the wavetable-folding passes reason about: its output
is provably zero past `end - start` samples *counting from the most
recent triggering input* — exactly the contract of the
`crag.finite = N` annotation — so an inlined-data one-shot chain can
fold into a `crag.lazy_wavetable` whose trigger-driven re-render +
playhead reset reproduces the retrigger semantics bit-exactly.
(Contrast `crag.sample`, whose `start` is an absolute position the
GRAPH advances per block — e.g. from `crag.curframe`; a
compile-time-constant `start` there replays the first block of the
slice every block and is NOT one-shot playback.)

Example — a kick one-shot fired from the host:

```mlir
%s  = crag.sampler "kick" : !crag.sampler<"kick">
%st = arith.constant 0    : i64
%en = arith.constant 9600 : i64
%fired, %at = crag.event_void "hit" infrequent : i1, i32
%audio = crag.sample_oneshot %s, %st, %en, %fired, %at
             : !crag.sampler<"kick">, i64, i64, i1, i32
               -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
```

| Operand | Description |
| :-----: | ----------- |
| `sampler` | crag sampler handle type |
| `start` | 64-bit signless integer |
| `end` | 64-bit signless integer |
| `fired` | 1-bit signless integer |
| `sample_offset` | 32-bit signless integer |

#### Results:

| Result | Description |
| :----: | ----------- |
| `out` | crag audio signal type |

entries.name: crag.sampler
entries.summary: Declares a named audio sampler handle
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.sampler` $name (`preferred_resampler` `=` $preferred_resampler^)? (`inlined_length` `=` $inlined_length^)? (`inlined_data` `=` $inlined_data^)? attr-dict `:` type($sampler) ``` Creates a handle to a named audio asset. The host binds audio data to the sampler by index using `crag_bind_audio_by_index`. Sampler names are listed in order of first appearance; the N-th unique name corresponds to index N-1 passed to `crag_bind_audio_by_index`. The optional `inlined_length` attribute records the total number of interleaved float samples in the WAV asset that was provided to `crag-compile` via `--inline-sampler`. When set, the compiler uses this value to derive the expected playback duration for `.cragmeta` output, marks the graph as deterministic (provided there are no `crag.param` ops), and emits a runtime sanity check that verifies the bound audio asset has the same length. The optional `inlined_data` attribute embeds the actual PCM byte array (as an `ElementsAttr` of `tensor`, interleaved samples) into the graph at compile time. When present, lowering emits a `constant memref.global` carrying the data, and `crag.sample` / `crag.sampler_length` ops read directly from it instead of from the runtime-bound pointer. The runtime ABI (ptr/len globals and `crag_bind_audio_by_index`) is still emitted unchanged so hosts that do rebind the asset continue to work, but the compiled binary no longer depends on a runtime bind for these samplers. This attribute is the prerequisite for compile-time analysis of sampler PCM (e.g. the periodic-folding pass that pre-analyzes wave-player asset data). Example: ```mlir %s = crag.sampler "drums" : !crag.sampler<"drums"> %s2 = crag.sampler "kick" inlined_length = 48000 : !crag.sampler<"kick"> %s3 = crag.sampler "blip" inlined_length = 4 inlined_data = dense<[0.0, 0.5, -0.5, 0.0]> : tensor<4xf32> : !crag.sampler<"blip"> ``` Traits: `AlwaysSpeculatableImplTrait` Interfaces: `ConditionallySpeculatable`, `NoMemoryEffect (MemoryEffectOpInterface)` Effects: `MemoryEffects::Effect{}` #### Attributes:

entries.name: crag.sampler_read
entries.summary: Read a single interleaved PCM sample from a bound sampler
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.sampler_read` $sampler `,` $index attr-dict `:` type($sampler) `,` type($index) `->` type($value)
```

Given a sampler handle and an interleaved sample index, returns the
single `f32` PCM value at that index from the bound audio asset.  The
index is a raw interleaved index (frame * channels + channel), matching
the units of `crag.sampler_length`.  When the index is out of bounds
(`idx < 0` or `idx >= sampler_length`) or no asset is bound, the result
is `0.0`.

Unlike `crag.sample`, which reads a contiguous block of `block_size`
samples into a `!crag.audio` value, `crag.sampler_read` performs a
single random-access scalar read.  This is the primitive used to
decimate an entire asset into an overview waveform (e.g. inside a
visualizer that draws the whole file the granulator is scrubbing).

Example:
```mlir
%s   = crag.sampler "audio" : !crag.sampler<"audio">
%len = crag.sampler_length %s : !crag.sampler<"audio"> -> i64
%mid = arith.divsi %len, %c2 : i64
%v   = crag.sampler_read %s, %mid : !crag.sampler<"audio">, i64 -> f32
```

entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.delay_line` attr-dict `:` type($delay) ``` Creates a handle to an N-channel circular delay-line buffer. entries.name: crag.peek_delay
entries.summary: Read an audio block from a delay line at a given sample offset without advancing the head
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.peek_delay` $delay `,` $offset attr-dict `:` type($delay) `,` type($offset) `->` type($out)
```

Reads `blockSize * channels` samples from the circular buffer starting
`offset` samples after the current write head and returns them as a
`!crag.audio` block.  Unlike `crag.pop_delay`, the write head is NOT
advanced and the buffer contents are NOT consumed.

The `offset` operand is an `i32` value in the range `[0, delaySize)`.
When `offset = 0` the behaviour is identical to `crag.pop_delay`
(reads the oldest stored samples).  Higher offsets skip further into
the buffer toward the most recently pushed data.

This is the fundamental building block for modulated-delay effects
such as chorus and flanger, where the read position is swept back and
forth within the delay buffer by an LFO.  The typical pattern is:

```mlir
// 1. Push new audio into the delay buffer.
crag.push_delay %d, %in
    : !crag.delay<f32, 48000, 1, 4800>, !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>

// 2. Compute the desired read offset from the head.
//    For a delay of D samples in a buffer of bufSize samples:
//      offset = bufSize - D
//    (reading bufSize - D samples ahead of the oldest data reads
//     the block that was pushed D samples ago.)
%offset = ...  // runtime i32 value in [0, delaySize)

// 3. Peek without moving the head.
%wet = crag.peek_delay %d, %offset
           : !crag.delay<f32, 48000, 1, 4800>, i32
             -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
```

Example (fixed 20 ms delay at 48 kHz, bufSize = 4800):
```mlir
%d      = crag.delay_line : !crag.delay<f32, 48000, 1, 4800>
%off    = arith.constant 3840 : i32   // 4800 - 960
crag.push_delay %d, %in : !crag.delay<f32, 48000, 1, 4800>,
                           !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>
%wet    = crag.peek_delay %d, %off
              : !crag.delay<f32, 48000, 1, 4800>, i32
                -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
```

| Operand | Description |

| `delay` | crag delay line type |
| `offset` | 32-bit signless integer |

| Result | Description |
| :----: | ----------- |

entries.body:

and returns them as a `!crag.audio` block.  The write head is not

```mlir
%delayed  = crag.pop_delay  %d : !crag.delay<f32, 48000, 1, 4096>
                -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
// ... process ...

                            !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
```

entries.name: crag.hard_clip
entries.summary: Clip each audio sample to the range [-threshold, threshold]
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.hard_clip` $input `,` $threshold attr-dict `:` type($input) `,` type($threshold) `->` type($out)
```

Applies hard clipping to every sample in the `!crag.audio` input block.
Each output sample is clamped to the symmetric range
[-threshold, +threshold]:

    y[n] = max(-threshold, min(+threshold, x[n]))

A `threshold` of 1.0 is the standard full-scale ceiling; smaller values
produce heavier clipping.  When `threshold` equals 0.0 the output is
all zeros; when it is very large (e.g. 1e9) the op is effectively
bypassed.

Hard clipping generates rich odd-order harmonic content, giving the
characteristic bright, aggressive tone of solid-state overdriven
amplifiers.

Example:
```mlir
%thresh = arith.constant 0.5 : f32
%clipped = crag.hard_clip %input, %thresh
               : !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>, f32 -> !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>
```

entries.name: crag.tanh
entries.summary: Apply tanh() soft saturation to each sample of an audio signal
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.tanh` $input attr-dict `:` type($input) `->` type($out)
```

Applies the hyperbolic tangent function to every sample in the
`!crag.audio` input block:

    y[n] = tanh(x[n])

Because tanh is a smooth, bounded S-curve (output always in (-1, 1))
it produces a continuous gradual compression of large amplitudes rather
than the abrupt cutoff of hard clipping.  The resulting distortion
has odd symmetry (tanh(-x) = -tanh(x)), so it generates only odd-order
harmonics (3rd, 5th, 7th …) for a symmetric input — giving a warm,
characteristically "tube-like" saturation quality.

To control the drive level, apply `crag.scale` before this op:
    driven = crag.scale input, drive   // amplify before tanh
    sat    = crag.tanh driven           // smooth saturation

The output amplitude for a pure sine input at drive D is
approximately tanh(D) ≤ 1.0, so no post-attenuation is needed for
unity-gain normalisation when drive ≤ 1.

Example:
```mlir
%drive  = arith.constant 2.0 : f32
%driven = crag.scale %input, %drive
              : !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>, f32 -> !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>
%sat    = crag.tanh %driven : !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0> -> !crag.audio<f32, 0, 0>
```

the oldest block without advancing, and `crag.peek_freq_delay` to
read any block by a runtime partition index.

entries.name: crag.freq_mul
entries.summary: Element-wise complex multiplication of two frequency-domain signals
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.freq_mul` $lhs `,` $rhs attr-dict `:` type($lhs) `,` type($rhs) `->` type($out)
```

Multiplies two `!crag.freq` blocks element-wise using complex
multiplication.  This is the core operation of FFT-based
convolution: given the FFTs of two signals A and B, their linear
convolution is `crag.ifft(crag.freq_mul(crag.fft(A), crag.fft(B)))`.

Both operands must have the same type.  The operation is lowered to
a `linalg.generic` over the underlying `tensor<N x complex<f32>>`
with `complex.mul` in the body, making full use of the MLIR complex
and linalg high-level dialects.

Example:
```mlir
%conv_freq = crag.freq_mul %dry_freq, %ir_freq
                 : !crag.freq<f32, 48000, 1>, !crag.freq<f32, 48000, 1>
                   -> !crag.freq<f32, 48000, 1>
```

entries.name: crag.overlap_save_conv
entries.summary: Partitioned overlap-save FFT convolution with dynamic partition count
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.overlap_save_conv` $dry `,` $ir_sampler `num_partitions` `=` $num_partitions attr-dict `:` type($dry) `,` type($ir_sampler) `->` type($out) ``` Implements a constant-complexity partitioned overlap-save FFT convolution between the live input `dry` and an impulse response loaded from `ir_sampler`. At each call (once per audio block), the op: 1. FFTs the input block and pushes it into an internal `numPartitions`-slot frequency-domain ring buffer. 2. Queries the bound IR length at runtime to compute `k = min(ceil(ir_len / blockSize), numPartitions)`. 3. For each partition `p` in `[0, k)`: - Reads input history block `p` from the ring buffer. - Reads IR partition `p` from the sampler. - FFTs the IR partition. - Multiplies the two frequency-domain blocks. 4. Accumulates all partition products and IFFTs to yield the output. Because exactly `numPartitions` FFT/multiply/IFFT operations are performed per block (partitions beyond `k` contribute zero when the sampler has less data), the per-block cost is constant regardless of IR length — this is the defining property of constant overlap-save. The `numPartitions` attribute sets the maximum number of partitions (compile-time constant); the actual `k` is determined at runtime from the sampler length. An IR of up to `numPartitions * blockSize` samples can be captured without aliasing across partition boundaries. Example: ```mlir %out = crag.overlap_save_conv %dry, %ir_sampler num_partitions = 16 : !crag.audio, !crag.sampler<"impulse_response"> -> !crag.audio ``` #### Attributes:
AttributeMLIR TypeDescription
num_partitions::mlir::IntegerAttr64-bit signless integer attribute
#### Operands: | Operand | Description | | :-----: | ----------- | | `dry` | crag audio signal type | | `ir_sampler` | crag sampler handle type | #### Results: | Result | Description | | :----: | ----------- | | `out` | crag audio signal type |

entries.name: crag.overlap_save_conv_slice
entries.summary: Partitioned overlap-save FFT convolution over a runtime IR slice
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.overlap_save_conv_slice` $dry `,` $ir_sampler `,` $ir_offset `,` $ir_length `num_partitions` `=` $num_partitions attr-dict `:` type($dry) `,` type($ir_sampler) `,` type($ir_offset) `,` type($ir_length) `->` type($out) ``` Variant of `crag.overlap_save_conv` that convolves the live input `dry` with a *runtime-selectable contiguous slice* of the IR sampler, rather than with the entire bound asset. This op supports runtime per-position HRIR selection: a single sampler holds many concatenated impulse responses and the host selects which one is active by passing `ir_offset = position_index * ir_length` and the per-position `ir_length` at audio-block granularity. Operands: - `dry` — live audio input. - `ir_sampler` — sampler holding the (concatenated) IR data. - `ir_offset` — `i64`, sample offset into the sampler at which the active IR begins. - `ir_length` — `i64`, length (in interleaved samples) of the active IR. Lowering follows `crag.overlap_save_conv` (FFT ring buffer of input history, partitioned IR FFT/multiply/IFFT) with two changes: 1. The runtime partition count `k` is computed from `ir_length` (clamped to `[1, num_partitions]`) instead of the whole sampler length. 2. IR partition `p` is read from sampler indices `[ir_offset + p*blockSize, ir_offset + (p+1)*blockSize)` with out-of-bounds samples zero-padded — exactly matching the `[ir_offset, ir_offset + ir_length)` window. `ir_offset` and `ir_length` may change across blocks; doing so causes a discontinuity in the IR identical to switching the bound sampler at block boundaries. Smoothing/cross-fading between positions is the host's responsibility (e.g. by sequencing two instances of this op and cross-fading their outputs). The `num_partitions` attribute, as in `crag.overlap_save_conv`, sets the maximum partition count and therefore the maximum per-block CPU cost; an `ir_length` larger than `num_partitions * blockSize` is silently truncated. Example (HRTF: pick position `i` of a pack of 256-sample IRs): ```mlir %ir_len = arith.constant 256 : i64 %i64 = arith.extsi %position_index : i32 to i64 %ir_offset = arith.muli %i64, %ir_len : i64 %wet = crag.overlap_save_conv_slice %dry, %ir_pack, %ir_offset, %ir_len num_partitions = 1 : !crag.audio, !crag.sampler<"hrir_pack_L">, i64, i64 -> !crag.audio ``` #### Attributes:
AttributeMLIR TypeDescription
num_partitions::mlir::IntegerAttr64-bit signless integer attribute
#### Operands: | Operand | Description | | :-----: | ----------- | | `dry` | crag audio signal type | | `ir_sampler` | crag sampler handle type | | `ir_offset` | 64-bit signless integer | | `ir_length` | 64-bit signless integer | #### Results: | Result | Description | | :----: | ----------- | | `out` | crag audio signal type |

entries.name: crag.peek_freq_delay
entries.summary: Read a frequency-domain block at a given partition offset
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.peek_freq_delay` $freq_delay `,` $partition_idx attr-dict `:` type($freq_delay) `,` type($partition_idx) `->` type($out)
```

Reads the frequency-domain block at partition offset `partition_idx`
from the head of the ring buffer without advancing the head.
`partition_idx = 0` reads the most recently pushed block;
`partition_idx = 1` reads the block pushed one call ago; and so on.

The `partition_idx` operand is an `i32` in the range
`[0, numPartitions)`.

This is the fundamental read operation for partitioned overlap-save
convolution: for partition `p` of the filter kernel, multiply
`crag.peek_freq_delay %fd, %p` with the FFT of the `p`-th kernel
partition and accumulate the result.

Example:
```mlir
%c0 = arith.constant 0 : i32
%newest = crag.peek_freq_delay %fd, %c0
    : !crag.freq_delay<f32, 48000, 1, 16>, i32
      -> !crag.freq<f32, 48000, 1>
```

entries.name: crag.tap_loop_conv
entries.summary: Time-domain (tap-loop) FIR convolution with runtime IR slice
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.tap_loop_conv` $dry `,` $ir_sampler `,` $ir_offset `,` $ir_length `max_length` `=` $max_length attr-dict `:` type($dry) `,` type($ir_sampler) `,` type($ir_offset) `,` type($ir_length) `->` type($out) ``` Direct-form FIR convolution that computes, for every output sample `n` in the current audio block: out[n] = sum_{k=0..ir_length-1} ir[ir_offset + k] * x[n - k] where `ir[...]` is read from `ir_sampler` (any sampler, typically bound to a pack of concatenated impulse responses) and `x[n - k]` is the input history maintained internally by the op. This is the "tap-loop convolution" alternative to the partitioned-FFT machinery: it sidesteps that machinery entirely in favour of reading IR samples directly via the same memory path as `crag.sample`, which makes it a natural building block for runtime per-position HRTF selection (and for the nearest-neighbour / linear-interpolation variants where `ir_length` is small enough that the O(blockSize · ir_length) direct form is cheaper than overlap-save). Operands: - `dry` — live audio input. - `ir_sampler` — sampler holding the IR data. - `ir_offset` — `i64`, sample offset into the sampler at which the active IR begins. - `ir_length` — `i64`, runtime number of taps to use. Clamped to `[0, max_length]` at runtime; values past `max_length` are truncated. The `max_length` attribute sets the compile-time upper bound on `ir_length` and therefore the size of the per-instance input history buffer (`max_length + blockSize - 1` samples per channel). `ir_offset` and `ir_length` may change across blocks; the input history buffer is preserved so the dry-side response is continuous across position changes (the IR side switches instantaneously, identical to swapping `crag.overlap_save_conv` IRs at a block boundary). Example (HRTF: pick position `i` of a pack of 256-sample IRs): ```mlir %ir_len = arith.constant 256 : i64 %i64 = arith.extsi %position_index : i32 to i64 %ir_offset = arith.muli %i64, %ir_len : i64 %wet = crag.tap_loop_conv %dry, %ir_pack, %ir_offset, %ir_len max_length = 256 : !crag.audio, !crag.sampler<"hrir_pack_L">, i64, i64 -> !crag.audio ``` #### Attributes:

entries.summary: Compute the peak (maximum absolute) amplitude of an audio block
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.peak` $input attr-dict `:` type($input) `->` type($value)
```

Returns the maximum absolute sample value across all samples in the
audio block as a scalar `f32`:

    peak = max( |x[i]| )   for all i in [0, blockSize × channels)

The result is always ≥ 0.  For silence the result is 0.0.

This op is the level-detection stage of a peak-following limiter or
compressor.  Combine it with `crag.smooth` to obtain a smoothed
peak envelope, then compute gain = min(1, threshold / envelope) for
limiting, and apply it with `crag.scale`.

Example:
```mlir
%pk = crag.peak %input : !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1> -> f32
```

entries.summary: Compute the root-mean-square amplitude of an audio block
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.rms` $input attr-dict `:` type($input) `->` type($value)
```

Computes the root-mean-square (RMS) amplitude of all samples in the
audio block and returns it as a scalar `f32` value.  For a block of N
total samples (blockSize × channels):

    rms = sqrt( sum(x[i]^2) / N )

The result is always ≥ 0.  For silence the result is 0.0.

This op is the level-detection stage of a feed-forward dynamics
processor (compressor, expander).  Combine it with `crag.smooth` to
obtain a smoothed envelope, compute gain reduction using `arith` /
`math` scalar ops, and apply the gain with `crag.scale`.

entries.name: crag.position_view
entries.summary: Render a 3D source position relative to a listener as an RGBA texture
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.position_view` $audio attr-dict `:` type($audio) `->` type($out) ``` Visualises a single 3D source position (typically the source position driving an HRTF spatializer) as a 2D projection of the listener-relative coordinate system. The listener sits at the centre of the image; the source is drawn as a colored dot at the projected position. Like `crag.compressor_viz`, this op reads its non-audio inputs from the tail of the per-visualizer audio capture buffer rather than as direct operands: the enclosing `crag.visualizer_ref` is expected to receive three additional `f32` operands after the audio operand — `(azimuth_rad, elevation_rad, distance_m)` — which the visualizer-ref lowering packs into `audioBuf[blockSize..blockSize+2]`. The audio operand itself is unused for rendering and exists only so the op can live inside a `crag.visualizer` body whose block argument is `!crag.audio`. The `view` attribute selects the projection: - `"top"` — top-down (above listener); axes: x → right, z → up. - `"side"` — left-of listener; axes: z → right, y → up. - `"rear"` — behind listener; axes: x → left, y → up. - `"combined"` — 2×2 tiled overlay of the three views above (top-left = top, top-right = side, bottom-left = rear). Spherical → Cartesian convention: `azimuth_rad` ∈ [-π, π] with 0 = front and +π/2 = right; `elevation_rad` ∈ [-π/2, π/2] with +π/2 = above; `distance_m` is clamped to a fixed display radius (so distant sources render at the edge of the projection circle). Example: ```mlir %img = crag.position_view %audio { view = "top" } : !crag.audio -> !crag.texture<256, 256> ``` Traits: `AlwaysSpeculatableImplTrait` Interfaces: `ConditionallySpeculatable`, `NoMemoryEffect (MemoryEffectOpInterface)` Effects: `MemoryEffects::Effect{}` #### Attributes:

```
operation ::= `crag.texture_read` $texture `,` $x `,` $y attr-dict `:` type($texture) `,` type($x) `,` type($y) `->` type($r) `,` type($g) `,` type($b) `,` type($a)
```

needs to do per-pixel math (e.g. alpha-blend a font-atlas glyph onto the
canvas, or read the canvas back before compositing).

```mlir

             : !crag.texture_sampler<"font"> -> !crag.texture<128, 128>
```

entries.name: crag.visualizer_ref
entries.summary: Reference a named crag.visualizer and capture audio for visualization
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.visualizer_ref` $viz_name `(` $inputs `)` attr-dict `:` `(` type($inputs) `)` ``` Captures the given audio signal for later visualization by the named `crag.visualizer`. This is a side-effect op: it stores the current audio block into a per-visualizer global buffer. The visualizer can then be run separately via the `crag_visualize(idx)` public API function to produce an image frame. The first operand must be the audio signal. An optional second operand may be supplied when the visualizer is a `crag.compressor_viz`: it should be the current gain-reduction value in dB (a negative f32 scalar). This extra value is packed into the last slot of the per-visualizer audio capture buffer where the impl function can read it. The audio operand may be a `!crag.audio<...>` type (when written in user IR before audio lowering) or a `tensor` (after the `crag-lower-audio-to-tensor` pass clones this op with the mapped tensor value). entries.name: crag.adsr
entries.summary: Sample-accurate one-shot ADSR envelope generator
entries.body:
Syntax:

```
operation ::= `crag.adsr` $attack_ms `,` $decay_ms `,` $sustain_level `,` $release_ms `,`
              $fired `,` $sample_offset
              attr-dict `:` type($attack_ms) `,` type($decay_ms) `,`
              type($sustain_level) `,` type($release_ms) `,`
              type($fired) `,` type($sample_offset) `->` type($out)
```

Generates an audio-rate Attack–Decay–Release envelope (A→D→R one-shot)
that responds to a sample-accurate trigger.  The output is a mono
`!crag.audio` block containing the envelope amplitude in [0, 1].

Trigger handling: when `fired` is `true`, the attack phase begins at
sample `sample_offset` within the current block, starting from the
current envelope level (allowing retriggering without a click).  The
envelope then proceeds automatically:
  1. **Attack** — ramps from the current level to 1.0 over `attack_ms`
  2. **Decay** — decays from 1.0 to `sustain_level` over `decay_ms`
  3. **Release** — decays from `sustain_level` to 0 over `release_ms`

After the release phase the envelope returns to idle (0.0) and waits
for the next trigger.  Persistent state (stage, phase, and the level
at which the last attack started) is maintained across `crag_process()`
calls.

Arguments:
  - `attack_ms`     — attack time in milliseconds (f32)
  - `decay_ms`      — decay time in milliseconds (f32)
  - `sustain_level` — sustain/decay target level in [0, 1] (f32)
  - `release_ms`    — release time in milliseconds (f32)
  - `fired`         — whether the trigger event fired this block (i1)
  - `sample_offset` — sample within the block where trigger fired (i32)

Example:
```mlir
%fired, %at = crag.event_void "trigger" : i1, i32
%atk  = crag.param "attack_ms"  min = 0.0 max = 10000.0 default = 10.0 unit = "ms" : f32
%dec  = crag.param "decay_ms"   min = 0.0 max = 10000.0 default = 100.0 unit = "ms" : f32
%sus  = crag.param "sustain"    min = 0.0 max = 1.0     default = 0.7 : f32
%rel  = crag.param "release_ms" min = 0.0 max = 10000.0 default = 200.0 unit = "ms" : f32
%env  = crag.adsr %atk, %dec, %sus, %rel, %fired, %at
            : f32, f32, f32, f32, i1, i32 -> !crag.audio<f32, 0, 1>
```

| `attack_ms` | 32-bit float |
| `decay_ms` | 32-bit float |
| `sustain_level` | 32-bit float |
| `release_ms` | 32-bit float |
| `fired` | 1-bit signless integer |
| `sample_offset` | 32-bit signless integer |

entries.name: crag.parallel
entries.summary: Sum a single audio body evaluated over N parallel lines
entries.body:
Evaluates one audio body region `count` times — once per *line* — and
returns the sum of the per-line results.  This collapses what would
otherwise be `count` hand-unrolled copies of identical IR (e.g. the
voices of a granular synth or the taps of a multitap delay) into a
single body parameterised by a line index.

The body's entry block receives the 0-based line index as its first
argument (`index`), followed by one scalar argument per `captures`
operand: capture `k` must be a 1-D tensor and the body sees its
`index`-th element.  This is how each line gets its own value for a
parameter — pass a `tensor<count x T>` of per-line values as a capture
and the body reads the element for its line.  The body may additionally
reference any SSA value from the enclosing region directly (ordinary
region capture), which is how lines share graph-wide params.

The body must terminate with `crag.parallel_yield`, whose type matches
the result type.  Lines are summed (`crag.sum` semantics), so a line
that should be silent must yield silence.

Lowering:
- When `count` is a compile-time constant (an `arith.constant` index),
  the `crag-unroll-parallel` pass fully unrolls and inlines the op:
  the body is cloned once per line with the index bound to a constant
  and each capture argument replaced by the corresponding constant
  tensor element, and the clones are summed with `crag.sum`.  Each
  clone therefore gets its own independent per-op state, exactly as if
  the lines had been written out by hand.
- When `count` is dynamic, `crag-lower-audio-to-tensor` lowers the op
  to an `scf.for` reduction that accumulates the per-line audio
  tensors.  (A sequential reduction is used rather than `scf.parallel`
  / `scf.forall` because per-line audio ops with persistent state share
  one state global across iterations when the line count is not known
  at compile time; see the note below.)

NOTE: prefer a constant `count` whenever possible.  Audio ops that carry
persistent state (delay lines, filters, oscillator phase) allocate that
state per op-identity; under dynamic unrolling every line reuses the
same state, which is only correct for stateless lines (pure samplers +
arithmetic, as in `granulator2`).

Example (4 detuned saw voices, each with its own detune ratio):
```mlir
%n      = arith.constant 4 : index
%ratios = arith.constant dense<[0.99, 0.997, 1.003, 1.01]>
              : tensor<4xf32>
%base   = crag.param "freq" min = 20.0 max = 2000.0 default = 110.0 : f32
%phase  = arith.constant 0.0 : f32
%mix = crag.parallel %n captures(%ratios : tensor<4xf32>)
           -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1> {
  ^bb0(%i: index, %ratio: f32):
    %f   = arith.mulf %base, %ratio : f32
    %saw = crag.saw %f, %phase
               : f32, f32 -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
    crag.parallel_yield %saw : !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
}
```

Selects one of N branch regions to evaluate and return as output, based
on the 0-based integer `selector` value.  Each branch is a region
containing audio-computing ops, terminated by `crag.selector_yield`.
Only the selected branch's result is forwarded; unselected branches are
dead code that may be eliminated by the compiler.

If `selector` is out of range (≥ number of branches), the last branch
is used.  The `selector` operand is typically produced by a
`crag.param_enum` op.

All branch yield types must match the result type.

Example:
```mlir
%wave = crag.param_enum "wave_type"
            values = ["sine", "saw", "square"]
            default = 0 : i32

%freq  = arith.constant 440.0 : f32
%phase = arith.constant 0.0   : f32
%duty  = arith.constant 0.5   : f32

%out = crag.selector %wave : i32 -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1> (
  {
    %sine = crag.sine %freq, %phase
                : f32, f32 -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
    crag.selector_yield %sine : !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
  }, {
    %saw = crag.saw %freq, %phase
               : f32, f32 -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
    crag.selector_yield %saw : !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
  }, {
    %square = crag.square %freq, %phase, %duty
                  : f32, f32, f32 -> !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
    crag.selector_yield %square : !crag.audio<f32, 48000, 1>
  })
```

entries.name: crag.func
entries.summary: Pure computation function region (non-audio inputs and outputs)
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.func` `name` `=` $func_name $body attr-dict ``` Defines a named, reusable computation function with non-audio inputs and outputs. Unlike `crag.graph`, a `crag.func` has no `sample_rate` or `channels` attributes and its body must **not** produce or consume `!crag.audio<...>` signals. The function body is a single-block region that ends with exactly one **void** `crag.func_return` op. The body may contain any `arith.*`, `math.*`, and `crag.*` ops that are valid in a graph body (including `crag.curframe`, `crag.block_size`, and nested `crag.func_ref` calls). A `crag.func` declares its inputs and outputs exclusively through **named pins** (the entry block has no `^bb0` arguments): - Inputs are declared by `crag.param*` / `crag.event*` ops. - Outputs are published by `crag.param_output*` / `crag.event_output*` ops, exactly as a graph declares its public control pins. Outputs flow through the output ops, so the terminating `crag.func_return` is always void. Named-pin functions can be discovered and placed as control-only graph-designer nodes. > The legacy positional `^bb0(...)` / value-returning `crag.func_return` > form was removed and is now rejected by the verifier. `crag.func` ops are eliminated by `crag-inline-funcs` before any lowering pass runs. Call sites use `crag.func_ref`, which binds its positional operands/results to the named pins in textual declaration order. Example: ```mlir crag.func name = "half_freq" { %freq = crag.param "freq" min = 0.0 max = 20000.0 default = 440.0 : f32 %two = arith.constant 2.0 : f32 %half = arith.divf %freq, %two : f32 crag.param_output "freq_out" %half : f32 crag.func_return } ``` #### Attributes:
AttributeMLIR TypeDescription
func_name::mlir::StringAttrstring attribute

The callee is identified by the string `callee` attribute and must be present in the same module. `crag.func_ref` ops are fully inlined by `crag-inline-funcs` before any lowering pass runs. Example: ```mlir // Call a function with two i32 inputs, one i1 and one i32 output. // (`metronome` is a named-pin crag.func: its two i32 control inputs // bind to these operands in textual order, and its `beat` event output // becomes the (fired, offset) results.) %fired, %offset = crag.func_ref "metronome"(%ref_sample, %period) : (i32, i32) -> (i1, i32) ``` Traits: `AlwaysSpeculatableImplTrait` Interfaces: `ConditionallySpeculatable`, `NoMemoryEffect (MemoryEffectOpInterface)` Effects: `MemoryEffects::Effect{}` #### Attributes:

entries.name: crag.struct_def
entries.summary: Declares a compile-time fixed-layout struct type
entries.body:
Syntax: ``` operation ::= `crag.struct_def` $sym_name attr-dict ``` Module-level op that declares a named, typed struct. The op is a compile-time artifact only and generates no code on its own. Fields are listed in declaration order; this order is authoritative for memory layout (C natural-alignment semantics). Allowed field element types are `f32`, `f64`, `i32`, `i64`, and `i1`. The op is used together with `crag.event_struct` (to declare an event that carries a struct payload) and with `crag.struct_create`, `crag.struct_get`, and `crag.struct_set` (to construct and inspect struct values inside graph bodies). The optional `field_mins` / `field_maxs` arrays carry advisory per-field value ranges for host display (e.g. so a `music_note.pitch` knob spans 0..127 rather than the generic default). When present each must hold one float entry per field, parallel to `field_names`; entries for `i1` fields are ignored. They are recorded in the `.cragmeta` file and do not affect layout, compilation, or runtime behaviour. Example: ```mlir crag.struct_def @music_note { field_names = ["pitch", "velocity"], field_types = [f32, f32], field_mins = [0.0, 0.0], field_maxs = [127.0, 1.0] } ``` #### Attributes:

entries.name: !crag.audio
entries.summary: Audio signal type
entries.body:
Audio stream contract used by CRAG graph processors.

The optional `subtype` attribute tags the signal with a semantic subtype
such as `"ambisonics"` or `"midside"`.  Operations like `crag.scale`,

```mlir

!crag.audio<f32, 48000, 9, subtype="ambisonics">    // second-order ambisonics (HOA2)
```
